reception.text: No newspaper coverage of the monument has been found, even in the digitized Daily Arizona Silver Belt of Globe, the Gila County seat.
reception.source: Chronicling America, 1907-08; California Digital Newspaper Collection, Dec. 1907-Mar. 1908

political_impact.text: The monument was placed under the Forest Service, which held it until 1933, though the ground lay outside the Tonto National Forest until January 1908.

legacy.text: The ruins were lightly guarded for two decades; the Forest Service and the Southern Pacific built the first road to them in 1929.
legacy.source: Nancy L. Dallett, At the Confluence of Change (2008)

legacy.text: Unsupervised visitors and vandals damaged the cliff dwellings at some point between the 1880s and the early 1930s; surviving records cannot fix when.
legacy.source: Dallett, At the Confluence of Change, p. 111

legacy.text: The first Park Service ranger, Charlie Steen, arrived in 1934.

today.name: Tonto National Monument
today.note: Now 1,120 acres: the original 640 plus 480 added in 1937.

related.note: The 1905 Tonto Forest Reserve, whose boundary left the monument's township outside it.
The January 1908 forest enlargement that brought the adjoining quarter-sections into the Tonto National Forest.

later_actions.text: The Forest Service and the Southern Pacific built a road, parking area and trail to the Lower Cliff Dwelling.
later_actions.source: Nancy L. Dallett, At the Confluence of Change (2008)

later_actions.text: Executive Order 6166 (signed June 10, 1933) transferred the monument to the National Park Service.
Franklin Roosevelt's Proclamation 2230 added about 480 acres from the Tonto National Forest and placed the monument under the Park Service director.

uncertain: Who first proposed Tonto as a national monument is not known.
Whether the proclamation met any objection is not known; government correspondence has not been read.
The Arizona Gazette, New York Times and Washington Post were not searched for coverage.
